subject: ventures/home-battery-planner
professional: a residential solar-plus-storage design engineer who sizes home batteries against customers' Green Button data and TOU/NBT tariffs; first checks: is each hour billed at the right import/export price (incl. holidays), are losses and inverter/reserve limits applied correctly, does the optimiser's ceiling match an exact LP, and do the controller modes behave like real self-powered / time-based settings

evidence.correctness: Recomputed outside the author's code (scratchpad hbp/indep.py, Python 3.13 + SciPy HiGHS, my own formulation). Example year, 13.5 kWh / 5 kW / 90% RT / 20% reserve: my hourly prices from the tariff text with my own 2025 OPM holiday list matched the tool's in 8,760 of 8,760 hours for plans A and B; bill without battery $2,018.82 (A) / $889.60 (B) = tool; my own self-powered replay $1,097.73 / $233.00 saving and 2,783.4 kWh delivered = tool exactly; my LP (charge <= spare solar, discharge <= load, 0 <= stored <= 10.8 kWh, eta = sqrt 0.9) gives $1,113.93 / $255.51, tool DP $1,113.88 / $255.51 (0.005% short, conservative as claimed). Hand TOU arbitrage: 3 days at 2 kWh/h, $0.10 off / $0.40 16-21, grid charging, reserve 0: time-based = 30 x 0.40 - (14.23 + 3 x 11.11) x 0.10 = $7.243 (tool 7.2436); ceiling 12 - (30/0.9) x 0.10 = $8.667 (tool DP 8.6616). 2026 holidays = OPM list less MLK/Juneteenth/Columbus (Jul 3 observed). Wrong outputs on reachable inputs: 'import 0-24: 0.50' is accepted with no error and prices no hour (all stay 0.30), and the Saturday New Year observance on Fri 2021-12-31 is filed under the next year's set and never applied.
evidence.completeness: README features checked end to end: CLI --example runs (three plans, five-size sweep, cheapest-plan lines); --json; Opower / delivered-received / SMT / ESPI readers exercised by tests; tariff features (wrap, last-wins, holidays, export import-minus, export tables, fixed) exercised; LP eval and ResStock tables present and the README/page numbers (97%, 25%, 40 of 40, -$12, $39, $239, $7/kWh) match check/resstock-results.md. Served copy (node platform/pages/served-copy.mjs) clean; live host 403 through the proxy. Not checked by the author and disclosed: a real utility Green Button file with solar.
evidence.verification: `node --test *.test.mjs` 32 pass in 3.6 s. The DP is guarded well (brute force on 20 random cases, lossless and lossy hand arbitrage, level convergence). Six mutants via quality_mutate.py: caught 3 (rule-mode reserve dropped, Saturday-holiday observance, DP grid charging forced on); survived 3 in shipped core paths: time-based grid-fill gate 'hi * roundTrip > lo' -> 'hi > lo', the grid-fill-after-solar branch 'used === 0 || x < 0' -> 'used === 0', and the meter's partial-hour scale-up removed. Time-based with grid charging and partial-hour scaling have no test.
evidence.craft: Read dispatch.mjs, tariff.mjs, meter.mjs, report.mjs, cli.mjs, example.mjs head, index.html and the guide. Small pure ES modules, documented invariants, one shared greenbutton.mjs pinned by a drift test. Defects: hourSet's loop cannot express 0-24 and fails silently; the observed-holiday date is put in the wrong year's set; runPeak takes 'days' as 24-hour blocks from the first reading rather than calendar days (measured effect under $1/yr on the example, offset 13 h: 212.82 vs 212.54); eval/lp-check-2026-11-18.md lists DP 1113.93 for the example where the current code gives 1113.88.
evidence.claims: Checked: 0.21% LP gap (eval doc, worst 0.207%), 97%/25%/40 of 40, Plan B -12/39/239, $7 per extra kWh, 32 cases, no upload / no key (page.test checks no fetch), disclaimer on both pages, invented prices labelled, limits list (netting, demand, wear, incentives). All backed. The guide carries the caveat that real time-based modes are smarter than the strict rule; the FAQ JSON-LD and on-page FAQ answer 'Self-powered or time-based mode?' with the strict rule's 25% and no such caveat.
evidence.fitness: Job: a solar owner or advisor with a year of Green Button data deciding whether a battery pays and in which mode. They get an honest per-hour replay and a sound ceiling, but: the time-based figure with grid charging ticked is not what any controller would do (example: $874 -> $213, because it fills from the grid at night and then spills the next morning's solar at $0.04); no NEM 2 monthly/annual netting (disclosed, but that is most existing California solar customers); no degradation, ITC/SGIP, or DC-coupled vs AC-coupled efficiency; a household 'thinking about' solar cannot add a PV profile. Usable as a first screen with the stated limits, not as a design deliverable.
evidence.domain: Matches practice: hourly import/export billing (NBT-style), sqrt(RT) split, reserve and inverter limits, perfect-foresight LP ceiling, 12x24 export tables like the CPUC ACC export-rate tables. Departs: time-based grid fill compares peak x RT with the cheapest import price but ignores that the alternative to grid charging is the day's spare solar worth the export credit, so it buys $0.33 energy and exports free solar; a single AC round trip for all paths (DC-coupled solar charging skips inverter losses); cycles counted against nameplate kWh rather than the reserve-limited span; no degradation or throughput warranty.

defects.what: Time-based mode with grid charging fills from the grid in every cheapest hour when peak x RT > cheapest import, ignoring that the day's spare solar (worth only the export credit) would fill it free; on the example year, Plan A, ticking 'May charge from the grid' cuts the time-based saving from $874 to $213 a year, a figure no real controller would produce and that steers the mode/permission choice.

Hour range 0-24 (a natural way to write 'all day') parses without error to an empty hour set, so 'import weekdays 0-24: 0.25' or 'export 0-24: x' silently prices nothing and the earlier line's price stands.

A Saturday New Year's Day is observed on the previous Friday, but that date is stored in the next year's holiday set and looked up in its own year's, so Fri 2021-12-31 (and 2027-12-31, 2032-12-31) are priced as weekdays.
Time-based grid fill and the meter's partial-hour scale-up are untested: three of six seeded mutants in those paths survive.

The FAQ (page and JSON-LD) answers 'Self-powered or time-based mode?' with the strict peak-only rule's 25% and no caveat that real time-based modes forecast and do better; the guide carries that caveat.
Time-based 'days' are 24-hour blocks from the first reading, not calendar days; a file starting mid-day shifts which hours count as each day's peak (under $1/yr on the example).
eval/lp-check-2026-11-18.md reports DP $1,113.93 for the example Plan A case; the current code gives $1,113.88.
Not modelled and a design engineer would ask first: NEM 2 monthly/annual netting (disclosed), DC-coupled solar charging efficiency, degradation/throughput, ITC/SGIP in payback.

verdict: The arithmetic is right where I could recompute it: my own pricing, billing, self-powered replay and HiGHS LP reproduce the example year exactly (prices 8,760/8,760, $2,018.82 bill, $1,097.73 self-powered, ceiling $1,113.88 vs LP $1,113.93), and hand TOU arbitrage matches (7.243 / 8.667). All README and page numbers match check/resstock-results.md. It does not meet the bar on verification: 32 tests pass and the DP is well guarded, but three of six seeded mutants in time-based grid fill and partial-hour scaling survive. A storage engineer would also reject the time-based-with-grid-charging rule ($874 -> $213 on the example because it buys grid energy ahead of free solar) and notice that 'import 0-24' is silently ignored.
